topics.title: 23.1 Pages
topics.summary: A page is a fixed-size unit in the virtual address space. A mapping associates a virtual page with backing storage and permissions. Pages should not be confused with C objects: a page can contain many objects, part of one object, or bytes that no live language object currently occupies. A large allocation can span many pages. Crossing its internal page boundaries is valid when the allocation and mappings permit it. Conversely, staying within one page does not prove an array index is valid. Object-level bounds and page-level mapping boundaries solve different problems.

topics.title: 23.2 Frames
topics.summary: A frame is a page-sized unit of physical storage. The kernel tracks which frames are free, in use, shared, or involved in other memory-management activity. A virtual page number and a physical frame number need not be equal. The distinction makes noncontiguous physical placement possible. Three adjacent virtual pages can be backed by frames 5, 200, and 9 while still appearing contiguous to the application. Device operations requiring particular physical arrangements need additional platform mechanisms; virtual contiguity alone is not a guarantee of physical contiguity.

topics.title: 23.3 Page size
topics.summary: For the following calculations, the page size is 4 KiB, or 4096 bytes. This is a teaching assumption, not a claim that every mapping on every system uses that size. Systems can support multiple page sizes, and applications should query the relevant platform interface where a runtime page size matters. Larger pages increase the amount of memory covered by one translation entry and reduce some table overhead. They can also waste more space for small or sparsely touched regions and complicate allocation or migration. The best size depends on workload and system policy, not merely on choosing the largest supported number.

topics.title: 23.4 Page offset
topics.summary: For a page size of 2^p bytes, the low p address bits form the page offset. With 4096-byte pages, p = 12 . The offset is address mod 4096 , or equivalently address & 0xFFF for the nonnegative integer model. Translation preserves these low bits when mapping a page to an equal-sized frame. Only the page-number portion changes. This separation makes the final physical-address calculation straightforward and explains why correctly aligned page bases have zeroes in the offset positions.

topics.title: 23.5 Virtual page number
topics.summary: The virtual page number is the address divided by page size, rounded down. In the bit model, it is address >> p . It identifies which page-table mapping applies, potentially through several levels of indexing. The number of bits available for the virtual page number depends on the virtual-address model. In a 32-bit model with 4-KiB pages, there are 20 virtual-page-number bits and 12 offset bits. Do not transfer those counts unchanged to a different address width or page size.

LECTURE NARRATION
Paging divides virtual address spaces and physical storage into fixed-size units. This simplifies placement: a virtual page can be backed by any suitable physical frame of the corresponding size. A frame is a page-sized unit of physical storage. The kernel tracks which frames are free, in use, shared, or involved in other memory-management activity.
